originalTitle: Feds can't withhold counterterrorism funds from states to force election admin changes, judge rules
summary: The judge said FEMA never explained how the election changes it wanted were "tied to the goal of shoring up vulnerabilities to terrorist attacks."
content:
A judge on Monday vacated a Trump administration rule that would withhold 20% of federal counterterrorism funds allocated for states unless states and certain municipalities made certain changes to how they administer elections.

In his ruling , U.S. District Court Judge Amir Ali said the Federal Emergency Management Agency exceeded its legal authority "by conditioning the counterterrorism grant funds on changes to routine election administration."

Ali also said FEMA , a division of the Department of Homeland Security , had not shown how the desired changes to election administration related to stopping terrorism.

Ali's decision in Washington, D.C., came in response to a lawsuit challenging FEMA's new rule, filed in August by counties in Texas and Tennessee, and the city of Columbus, Ohio.

The Brennan Center for Justice at New York University , which represents some of the plaintiffs in the suit against FEMA and DHS, said on Aug. 17 that FEMA's conditions "violate the Constitution, jeopardize public safety, and put election security at risk."

"Over the last two years, courts have largely blocked the administration's repeated attempts to seize congressional and state authority over elections," the Brennan Center said at the time. "Now, DHS is holding public safety funding hostage in order to coerce states and local governments into adopting some of the very policies that the administration has tried and failed to impose."

The Brennan Center said the funds that stood to be withheld if FEMA's conditions were allowed to remain in place totaled tens of millions of dollars.

Read more CNBC politics and policy coverage

A spokesman for the Department of Justice, which represented DHS and FEMA, declined to comment on Ali's ruling.

Abbie Kamin, the County Attorney of Harris County, Texas, said in a statement, "Today's win is the result of cities and counties standing together against blatant federal overreach that jeopardized public safety."

"The court agreed that holding public safety funding hostage to force the president's agenda is dangerous and illegal," said Kamin, whose county was one of the plaintiffs in the case. "Under our laws, states and localities control our elections, and today's ruling reaffirms that."

FEMA issued the rule in June requiring states "and their respective high-risk urban areas" to make certain changes to election administration or face the withholding of 20% of a state's allocation of counterterrorism funds from the federal government, Ali noted.

Urban areas in the U.S. vote overwhelmingly for Democrats.

The changes include submitting a plan for transitioning from electronic voting systems that use bar codes or QR codes to hand-marked paper ballots; conducting, under federally specified guidelines, a post-election manual audit of 5% of the ballots; and ensuring that each election jurisdiction reconciles the number of voters who voted in a federal election to the number of ballots cast.

The required changes also include verifying the U.S. citizenship of all voters in the state's registration database, and the citizenship of poll workers, election administrators and election-system vendors.

Ali, in his ruling, said, "FEMA's conditions here — which are imposed on states and localities at their own expense, rather than funded by grants, and which address routine election administration decisions rather than the types of terrorist act threats contemplated by the statute — go beyond what Congress authorized."

"For example, the defendants say the ... condition requiring states to adopt FEMA's proposed citizenship-verification procedures in maintaining lists of registered voters 'ensures that only U.S. citizens are voting in U.S. elections,'" Ali wrote.

"But it never explains how that condition, or any of the others, is tied to the goal of shoring up vulnerabilities to terrorist attacks," the judge said.
chineseTitle: 法官规定，美联储不能扣留各州的反恐资金以迫使选举管理机构发生变化
chineseSummary: 法官表示，联邦应急管理局从未解释过它想要的选举改变是如何“与加强恐怖袭击脆弱性的目标联系在一起的”。
chineseContent:
周一，一名法官撤销了特朗普政府的一项规定，该规定将扣留分配给各州的联邦反恐资金的 20%，除非各州和某些市政府对选举管理方式做出某些改变。

美国地方法院法官阿米尔·阿里在裁决中表示，联邦紧急事务管理局“根据常规选举管理的变化来调整反恐拨款”，从而超出了其法律权限。

阿里还表示，国土安全部下属的联邦应急管理局没有表明选举管理的预期变化与制止恐怖主义有何关系。

阿里在华盛顿特区做出的决定是对德克萨斯州、田纳西州各县以及俄亥俄州哥伦布市于 8 月提起的质疑联邦应急管理局新规定的诉讼的回应。

代表部分原告起诉 FEMA 和 DHS 的纽约大学布伦南司法中心 8 月 17 日表示，FEMA 的条件“违反宪法，危害公共安全，并使选举安全面临风险”。

布伦南中心当时表示：“过去两年，法院在很大程度上阻止了政府一再试图夺取国会和州对选举的权力。” “现在，国土安全部正在扣押公共安全资金，以迫使各州和地方政府采取一些政府曾尝试但未能实施的政策。”

布伦南中心表示，如果联邦应急管理局的条件得以维持，则将被扣留的资金总计数千万美元。

阅读更多 CNBC 政治和政策报道

代表国土安全部和联邦应急管理局的司法部发言人拒绝对阿里的裁决发表评论。

德克萨斯州哈里斯县检察官艾比·卡明在一份声明中表示，“今天的胜利是各市县共同反对联邦政府公然越权危害公共安全的结果。”

卡明是本案原告之一，他所在的县是该案的原告之一。 “根据我们的法律，州和地方控制我们的选举，今天的裁决重申了这一点。”

阿里指出，联邦紧急事务管理局 (FEMA) 于 6 月发布了该规定，要求各州“及其各自的高风险城市地区”对选举管理进行某些改变，否则将面临联邦政府扣留各州 20% 反恐资金的拨款。

美国城市地区绝大多数投票给民主党。

这些变化包括提交一份从使用条形码或二维码的电子投票系统过渡到手写纸质选票的计划；根据联邦指定的指导方针，对 5% 的选票进行选举后人工审核；确保每个选举辖区将在联邦选举中投票的选民人数与所投选票的数量进行核对。

所需的改变还包括验证该州登记数据库中所有选民的美国公民身份，以及投票站工作人员、选举管理员和选举系统供应商的公民身份。

阿里在裁决中表示，“联邦应急管理局的条件——这些条件是由各州和地方自费强加的，而不是由赠款资助的，并且涉及例行的选举管理决定，而不是法规设想的恐怖主义行为威胁的类型——超出了国会的授权。”

阿里写道：“例如，被告称……要求各州采用联邦应急管理局提议的公民身份验证程序来维护登记选民名单的条件，‘确保只有美国公民才能在美国选举中投票’。”

“但它从未解释这种情况或任何其他情况如何与加强恐怖袭击脆弱性的目标联系在一起，”法官说。
